items.title: Buster Williams interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002
items.q: One of the things that Herbie Hancock and Wayne Shorter and Ron Carter, since when you’re talking about Herbie and Wayne and Ron, you know you don’t have to use their last names, everybody knows who you’re talking about.

ctx.x: Yeah. You know a friend of mine, we were just talking about that the other day. One of the things that Herbie Hancock and Wayne Shorter and Ron Carter, since when you’re talking about Herbie and Wayne and Ron, you know you don’t have to use their last names, everybody knows who you’re talking about. One of the things that perpetrated their music was the fact that they played each other’s music. And that’s sort of the kind of thing that Bird and Monk and Miles and Dizzy, they did also. They played each other’s…
I think it helps too if there’s a lyric.

items.title: Ron Carter — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So when I put the band together, I said maybe I'd hire Buster and try to get Ben.

ctx.x: You've mentioned the two-bass quartet and I'm also looking at a note here that says the piccolo. Talk to me a little bit about those concepts. It was something different you did.

Well, when I wanted to be a bandleader, I just wanted to be in front of the band physically. My feeling was that if you walk into the room with a trio – piano, bass and drums – people automatically assume this is a piano player's trio. And that's what that is, you know. But I wanted an instrument that would put me in front of the band, and so I put a bass player in the band. So the choices were either stand in front of the band physically, way out here in front of the band, or have the band here and help me…

I've always loved Ben Riley's playing and I thought Buster was the kind of guy who would be able to accompany a bass player and not be bent out of shape because his musicality is so high. Buster's a great sideman, by the way. So, I said, "Well, let me get a band together," and I had known Kenny from playing two dates with him, with Dizzy and Yusef. Occasionally, Miles would work opposite those bands and we'd be a block away and I'd get a chance to hear them. Then there was late Brother Bill, the saxophone player.…
